nameStory: The Northern Moonsnail gets its dreamy name from its perfectly round, moon-like shell that gleams with a pearlescent sheen when wet. Like the moon itself, this snail emerges from the depths to hunt in the shallows, though it's more commonly found in deeper waters below the low tide line.
description: The Northern Moonsnail is a large, impressive sea snail with a smooth, globe-shaped shell that can grow quite substantial in size. Its shell is typically grayish-brown to tan in color with a glossy finish that catches the light beautifully when wet. This hefty marine mollusk is a powerful predator that spends most of its time in deeper waters, though beachcombers occasionally find empty shells washed up on shore. When alive, the snail's body is much larger than its shell and appears almost too big to fit inside.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Perfectly round and globe-like when viewed from above, smooth as a polished marble with no ridges or bumps to catch your finger

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Grayish-brown to tan coloration with a glossy, almost porcelain-like finish that feels smooth and cool to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably large for a snail shell - feels substantial and weighty in your palm, much bigger than common periwinkles

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: Wide, oval-shaped opening (aperture) that takes up most of one side of the shell, large enough to stick your thumb into

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Shell surface is completely smooth with fine growth lines you can barely feel with your fingertip, no spines or rough patches

habitat: Northern Moonsnails prefer sandy and muddy bottoms in deeper coastal waters below the low tide line, though empty shells often wash up on New England beaches. They're most common in subtidal zones where they hunt for clams and other mollusks, burrowing through soft sediments in bays, harbors, and offshore areas.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells begin washing up on beaches after winter storms, often the best time to find fresh specimens with intact shells.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding shells on beaches during low tides, though living snails remain in deeper waters offshore.
seasonality.fall: Continued shell washing with autumn storms, shells may show more wear from summer wave action.
seasonality.winter: Fewer shells found due to harsh conditions, but winter storms occasionally deposit large, well-preserved specimens.

funFact: Northern Moonsnails are voracious predators that drill perfectly round holes through clam shells using their rasping tongue (called a radula) - if you find a clamshell with a neat circular hole, you're looking at evidence of a moonsnail's handiwork!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the Spotted Moonsnail, but Northern Moonsnails lack the distinctive rows of spots and are generally larger and more uniformly colored. Remember: "Northern = no spots, Spotted = small spots in rows."
compareHints: Northern Moonsnails are larger and lack the characteristic spiral rows of dark spots found on their close relative, the Spotted Moonsnail. While Spotted Moonsnails have distinctive dotted patterns that look almost painted on, Northern Moonsnails maintain a solid, uniform coloration across their entire shell. Northern Moonsnails also tend to be more robust and hefty-feeling compared to the more delicate Spotted Moonsnail.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spotted moonsnails are much smaller than their close relative, the Northern moonsnail, and have the distinctive three rows of spots that Northern moonsnails lack.
